title: Java Documentation Comments
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of java documentation comments and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—/**... */ comments—in a small, readable example.
Predict the example result and check it against the stated output or a boundary-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study java documentation comments with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you choose types and variable scope deliberately instead of relying on guesses about values. In this lesson, focus on /**... */ comments and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Java variables have declared or inferred static types and a defined scope. Local `var` infers a compile-time type from the initializer; it does not make the language dynamically typed. Apply that reasoning specifically to /**... */ comments and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect /**... */ comments with @param, @return, and @throws before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: @param, @return, and @throws
items.text: Exceptions report conditions that interrupt the normal path. Catch only when the code can recover or add context, preserve the original cause, and use try-with-resources for closeable resources.

items.title: Linking to other API documentation
items.text: Use Path and Files for modern file operations, choose byte or character APIs based on the data, and close resources reliably. Parse external files defensively because their contents may be incomplete or malformed.

items.title: Documenting public classes and methods
items.text: A method gives a named contract to a unit of behavior. Keep responsibilities focused, define clear parameter and return types, and test typical, boundary, and invalid cases independently.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Add documentation where it clarifies a public contract or a non-obvious decision. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.

common_mistakes.problem: Applying the rule from memory without checking its exact contract.
common_mistakes.why: Small differences in type, scope, API version, or input shape can change the result.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the relevant official API/language documentation and build a minimal reproducer.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
